subject: ENG
label: Grade 11 Humanities
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 11 Humanities English, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 5 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Prose and poetry from world writers
modules.outcome: analyse theme and voice in two texts
modules.intro: In this unit, 'Prose and poetry from world writers', you learn to analyse theme and voice in two texts. You work with exam-style questions and written reasoning. You see it, say it, then do it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Prose and poetry from world writers' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: analyse theme and voice in two texts, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Simile: 'The moon is like a silver coin.' Metaphor: 'The classroom was a zoo.' Imagery: 'the dew-wet grass' appeals to sight and touch. Say what feeling each creates. Method: Model run for 'Prose and poetry from world writers'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Analyse theme and voice in two texts: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Read Text A, a prose extract. 'At the station, Ravi held his suitcase as if it were a small, frightened animal. Everything in the city was louder than he had been warned. He practised the new name of his street under his breath.' Note the narrator's close, gentle voice.

Step 2, Read Text B, a poem. 'My grandmother drew the village from memory: / the well, the mango tree, the school. / The map had no scale, no north, / and every road led home.' Both texts concern leaving a place and holding on to it in the mind.

Step 3, Name the theme of each. Text A: arriving in a strange place brings fear and a wish to belong. Text B: memory can map a lost home more truly than a real map. Shared theme: belonging and displacement. Write each in a full sentence and keep it general, not a plot summary.

Step 4, Analyse voice. In Text A the close third-person narrator uses the simile 'a small, frightened animal' to show Ravi's fear, and 'under his breath' shows he is shy. In Text B the speaker's calm, affectionate voice listing 'the well, the mango tree, the school' shows love through small details.

Step 5, Write a comparison. 'Both texts present belonging as fragile. In Text A, Ravi holds his suitcase "as if it were a small, frightened animal", while in Text B the grandmother's map "had no scale, no north" but led "home". Ravi fears the new; the grandmother treasures the old.' Quote precisely.

Step 6, Your turn: explain 'every road led home'. Model answer: It is a metaphor suggesting that, in memory, every path returns to the lost village. It shows how deeply the grandmother belongs to her home, even though she can no longer visit it.

modules.title: Grammar and editing
modules.outcome: edit text for tense, agreement and clarity
modules.intro: In this unit, 'Grammar and editing', you learn to edit text for tense, agreement and clarity. You work with exam-style questions and written reasoning. You see it, say it, then do it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Grammar and editing' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: edit text for tense, agreement and clarity, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Passive: 'The cat chased the mouse' becomes 'The mouse was chased by the cat.' Reported: 'I will come,' she said becomes She said that she would come. Modals: 'should' for advice, 'must' for rules. Agreement: 'The list of items is long.' Edit: 'He go to school' becomes 'He goes to school.' Method: Model run for 'Grammar and editing'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Edit text for tense, agreement and clarity: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Edit for tense. Passage: 'Last year the village build a new school and celebrates its opening.' 'Last year' demands the past tense, so write 'built a new school and celebrated its opening'. Underline time clues first and check every verb in the sentence against them.

Step 2, Edit for agreement. 'The history of these towns are interesting.' The subject is 'history', singular, so write 'is interesting'. 'One of the museums have closed' becomes 'has closed'. 'Neither the guide nor the visitors was tired' becomes 'were tired', matching the nearer subject.

Step 3, Edit for clarity. 'Having crossed the river, the temple came into view.' The temple did not cross the river. Rewrite: 'Having crossed the river, we saw the temple.' Place the modifier next to the person it describes. Another: 'The mayor told the officer that he was late' needs a clear 'he'.

Step 4, Remove repetition. 'The reason why the revolution happened was because of hunger' becomes 'The revolution happened because of hunger.' 'In my personal opinion I think' becomes 'I think'. Choose the shortest clear wording that keeps the meaning.

Step 5, Edit a short passage. Original: 'The people was angry, so they marches to the capital and demand change, which were reasonable.' Edited: 'The people were angry, so they marched to the capital and demanded change, which was reasonable.' Check each verb against the subject and the time frame.

Step 6, Your turn: correct 'The group of historians were studying the old letters that has been found.' Answer: 'The group of historians was studying the old letters that had been found.' 'Group' is singular, and 'letters' needs 'had been found' for the earlier event.

modules.title: Writing: speeches, articles and reports
modules.intro: In this unit, 'Writing: speeches, articles and reports', you learn to write persuasive and informative pieces. You work with exam-style questions and written reasoning. You see it, say it, then do it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Writing: speeches, articles and reports' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: write persuasive and informative pieces, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Formal letter: 12 November 2026; The Principal; Subject: request for a library card; 'Respected Sir, I am a student of Class 8...'; Yours faithfully, Aman. Informal: Dear Ria, ... Your friend, Aman. Report: title, date, place, what happened, result, writer's name. Method: Model run for 'Writing: speeches, articles and reports'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Write persuasive and informative pieces: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Fix purpose and audience. Task: persuade the local council to keep the town library open on Sundays. Audience: council members. Persuasive writing needs a clear claim, evidence and a call to action. Informative writing, such as a report, needs facts in a neutral order. Choose the tone: respectful, formal, firm.

Step 2, Work out the evidence. A survey of 250 residents found 150 in favour: 150 divided by 250 is 60 percent. Sunday visits in a trial month were 480 against 400 on a normal weekend: 80 divided by 400 is 20 percent more. These figures are your strongest evidence.

Step 3, Write the speech. 'Honourable members, imagine a Sunday when the doors of our library are closed and a hundred students have nowhere quiet to study. Sixty percent of residents want Sunday opening.' Add 'Visits rose by 20 percent in our trial.' A hook, then a fact, builds trust.

Step 4, Write the article version. Headline: 'Sunday Opening Wins Public Support'. By-line. First paragraph: 'Most residents want their library open on Sundays, a recent survey suggests.' Use quotations and statistics, and end with what readers can do next. Articles inform while gently arguing.

Step 5, Write a short report. Sections: title, introduction, findings, recommendation. Findings: '60 percent of 250 respondents support Sunday opening. Weekend visits rose by 20 percent in the trial.' Recommendation: 'Open the library on Sundays for six months and review the results.' Stay neutral and precise.

Step 6, Your turn: a survey of 120 residents shows 90 want a new bus route. Write the finding. Answer: 'Of the 120 residents surveyed, 90, or 75 percent, want a new bus route.' Check: 90 divided by 120 is 0.75.

modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Answer inference and evaluation questions: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Read my own passage. "In the village archive, the clerk guarded the old registers as if they were relatives. Nobody asked why she never let anyone borrow them; the dust on the shelves said enough." Gist: she values the past and keeps it secure.

Step 2, Locate evidence. "Guarded...as if they were relatives" is a simile that suggests deep attachment. "The dust on the shelves said enough" implies the registers are rarely touched. Reason: quote briefly, then comment.

Step 3, Answer an inference question. "What does the clerk's behaviour suggest?" Model: "It suggests she feels responsible for the community's memory, since she treats the registers like family." Reason: an inference goes beyond what is stated.

Step 4, Evaluate language effects. "How does personification in 'the dust said enough' affect the reader?" Model: "It gives silent objects a voice, which creates a quiet, sad mood and implies neglect."

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak: "The writer uses a simile to make it better." Right: "The simile compares registers to relatives, which suggests affection and emotional value." Always explain effect, not just a label.

Step 6, Read a poem, my own: "The river keeps the town's old names, / and carries them to sea." Inference: time carries memories away. Evidence: "carries them to sea" suggests loss. Tone: wistful, reflective.

Step 7, Your turn. Passage: "Though the festival had ended, the lanterns still hung in the empty street." What mood is created and how? Model answer: "A lonely, nostalgic mood; 'still hung' and 'empty' contrast with the festival's past liveliness."

modules.standard: Deliver a structured speech and respond to questions: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Plan with a clear thesis. Topic: "Local history should be taught in schools." Thesis: "Studying local history gives students identity and critical skills." Outline: hook, thesis, three points, counter-argument, conclusion.

Step 2, Write a persuasive hook. "Do you know who built the bridge you cross every morning? Most of us don't, and that silence says something about what we teach." Reason: a question draws listeners in.

Step 3, Develop a point with an example and a reason. "First, local history builds identity. For example, learning how our market began shows students that ordinary people shape history." Reason: example plus reason convinces.

Step 4, Use rhetorical devices with purpose. Triad: "to remember, to question and to rebuild." Contrast: "not only the kings, but also the carpenters." Reason: devices create rhythm and emphasis, but they must support the argument.

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak: "History is very important and everyone says so." Better: "History trains students to weigh evidence, and that skill applies to every subject." Remove vague claims; give a specific benefit.

Step 6, Answer a question with a structure. Q: "Isn't world history more useful?" A: "World history matters, but local history makes it real; students connect national events to places they know." Reason: concede, then argue.

Step 7, Your turn. Write a thesis and one counter-argument response for "Public libraries remain essential". Model answer: "Thesis: Libraries give equal access to knowledge." "Response: Online resources help, but not everyone has devices or connection."
